messages.content: what is the difference between very much and too much when talking about food?
in i like rice very much, very much is about how much you like it. in i ate too much rice, too much is about eating more than you wanted or needed. the words do different work in those sentences.
explain simply.
very much can say how much you like food. too much can say you ate more food than you wanted.
write a short conversation where one person has too much rice on a plate.
would you like more rice? no, thank you. i already have too much. should i take some away? yes, please. i only wanted a small meal.
does too much mean the person does not like the rice?
no. it is about how much is on the plate. the person could like the rice but still want less.
answer simply.
no. they may like the rice but have more than they want.
can you make an example with tea that is too cold for someone?
the tea is cold, and i would like it warm. it is too cold for me to enjoy now.
does that mean nobody can enjoy cold tea?
no. for me keeps the idea about that person. another person may enjoy it cold.
can moving only change the meaning of a sentence?
yes. only can go with different parts of a sentence. only i read the book is about who read it. i only read the book can be about what you did, rather than writing about it or doing something else.
give a small example with a brother and sister.
only my sister read the book. i drew a picture while she read. that says she was the one reading that book, rather than me.
can i have read another book?
yes. only my sister read the book is about that specific book. it does not say you never read anything else.
now use i read the book too.
my sister read the book, and i read it too. that says both people read the same book.
does too mean we read it at the same time?
no. it gives another person who read it. you could have read on different days.
answer simply.
no. both people read it, but the sentence does not say when each person read.
write one sentence making different days clear.
my sister read the book yesterday, and i read it today.
write a first conversation with someone new at school. do not say we have met before.
hello. may i sit here? yes, the chair is free. thank you. do you come here to read often? sometimes. today i am working on a story. what is it about? a child who visits another town.
visits is in the list, but can you make the story idea more simple?
a child goes to another town.
what should i do if the other person only wants to work quietly?
you can leave them room to do that. you might say: i will read quietly too. tell me if you would rather have this table to yourself.
can i still be kind without asking more questions?
yes. a first conversation does not need to be long. saying hello and giving someone space can be enough.
write a short line to end it before reading.
it was nice to meet you. i will read for a while now.
does nice to meet you say we will be close friends?
no. it is a kind way to finish a first conversation. it does not tell us how much time you will spend together later.
answer simply.
no. it is kind, but it does not tell us how much time you will spend together later.
i write please bring one book on a note and give it to two people. do i need to say whether i want one from each?
yes, if the number is important. one book could be for two people to bring together, or you might mean one from each person. make the number clear.
use important in a simple answer.
if the number is important, say whether you want one book together or one from each person.
write one message for each of those plans.
please bring one book for us to share. please each bring one book.
tell me what i asked for simply.
you asked for one example with one book and another with a book from each person.
use one in a short answer.
one example has one book together. the other asks each person for a book.
if there are two people, how many books in the plan asking each person for one?
two books, if each brings one.
answer with the plan for each.
the plan asking each person for a book gives two books from two people.
tell me a short story about someone walking to a library on a warm day.

a woman walks to the library with a book to return. the day is warm, so she stops under a tree for a moment before going inside. at the desk, she asks whether the next part of the story is there. a worker brings another book, and she looks at the first page before choosing it.
now change the warm day to a cold day, but keep her going to return a book.

a woman walks to the library with a book to return. the day is cold, so she goes inside right away. at the desk, she asks whether the next part of the story is there. a worker brings another book, and she looks at the first page before choosing it.
give just the sentence about the cold day.
the day is cold, so she goes inside right away.
use sitting to say what she does not do under the tree.
the day is cold, so she goes inside instead of sitting under the tree.
did changing the weather take away the book return?
no. both stories keep her reason for going: returning a book. the weather changes one part of how she gets there, not that goal.
answer simply.
no. she still goes to return the book in both stories.
my family wants a meal together, but nobody has asked my sister if she is free. can we say everyone chose the time?
not yet. your sister still needs to answer before saying the time works for everyone.
answer simply.
not yet. you still need your sister to answer.
write a question for her using tomorrow evening.
would tomorrow evening work for a family meal?
she says she is free, but our father now has work then.
then the time does not work for everyone yet. one person being free does not mean every person is free. your father still has work, so the group needs another choice.
say it simply.
one person being free does not mean every person is free. your father still has work, so the group needs another choice.
can we choose a time for most people rather than everyone?
you can choose a time most people can come, but should not call it a time everyone can come.
answer simply.
yes, but say it is for most people, rather than everyone.
write a story where a child asks for a cup, and the father asks whether the child wants to use it or keep it.

a child asks if she can have a cup from the kitchen. her father asks what she needs it for. she wants to put her drawing tools in it. he says she can use it that afternoon, but it is still a cup for the kitchen. she had thought have was about keeping it in her room. they talk again and choose an empty container she can keep for the tools. the cup is still in the kitchen, and her tools have a place in her room.
make the last part simple.
she thought she could keep it, but he said she could only use it for that afternoon. they choose another container for the tools.
say what he said in a short answer.
he said she could only use the cup for that afternoon.
what question would have helped at the start?
do you want to use the cup for a while, or keep it for your tools?
does choosing another container mean the child was wrong to ask?
no. the request helped them learn what she wanted and find something that worked. a question can need more context without being wrong to ask.
ask my last question simply.
does asking for something that does not work mean she was wrong to ask at all?
here is a sentence: i found a note and read it at the table. change it so i am telling someone what they did.
you found a note and read it at the table.
now make it about a group with me in it.
we found a note and read it at the table.
does we tell us who read the words so everyone could hear?
not always. we read it can mean each person looked at it, or that one person read for the group. you need more detail if that difference is important.
use so everyone could hear in my question.
does we tell us who read so everyone could hear?
make it clear i read while the other people listened.
we found a note, and i read it at the table while the other people listened.
can i say they read it if they only listened?
to keep the detail clear, say that you read and they listened. that keeps what each person did clear.
answer simply.
say that you read and they listened. those are different things in the story.
say it simply.
you read. they listened.
if an answer is short and easy to read, is it always a good answer?
no. it still needs to answer the question and keep the facts right. a short answer can leave out needed information or say something wrong very clearly.
make a simple example with a book on a desk.
where is the book? on the shelf. that reply is short, but if the book is on the desk, it is wrong. on the desk is short and correct for that fact.
what if the question was what color is the book?
then on the desk does not answer the question, even if the place is right. you need the color, or you need to say that you do not know it.
write an answer if you know only the place and not the color.
i know the book is on the desk, but i do not know its color.
can saying i do not know be better than choosing blue without information?
yes. saying what you know and what you do not know keeps the answer clear. blue would add a fact you do not have.
ask my last question simply.
can saying i do not know be better than choosing blue without information?
now give a very short answer about the color, using only what you know.
i do not know the color.
say my request simply.
give a very short answer about the color, using only what you know.
a note on a table says go home. does that tell every person who sees it to leave?
not without context. the note may be for one person, for a game, or part of something else. you need to know who wrote it and who should read it.
write a short story where it is part of a made up game.

a child writes go home on a card and puts it next to a toy house. her brother thinks it is a message for him and asks why he has to leave. she says it is for a person in her game, not for him. he sits down and asks what the game person will do next. she moves the small toy to the toy house, and they keep making the story together.
use next to and small toy in the story.
she puts the card next to a toy house. later, she moves the small toy to that house as part of the story.
why did the brother need more context?
he saw the words but did not know who they were for. the same words can be a request for someone or only writing inside a story.
answer simply.
he knew the words, but not who they were for. the child explained that the note was part of a game.
does reading a request mean it is always a request for you?
no. you need context to know who the words are for.
say it simply.
no. you need context to know who the words are for.
my friend said they wanted to walk, then later said they wanted to stay home. does that mean the first answer was false?
not always. people can change what they want. you would need more information to know whether the first answer was false when they gave it.
ask and answer simply.
changing a choice does not always mean the first answer was false. the person may want something different now.
what can i say if i am still happy to visit them at home?
would you like me to come over instead of going for a walk?
what if i wanted to walk more than i wanted a visit?
then give a kind answer about your own plan: i think i will still go for a walk today. we can visit another time if you would like.
write just the reply.
i think i will still go for a walk today. we can visit another time if you would like.
does that mean we are not friends now?
no. choosing different things for one afternoon does not by itself end time together as friends.
answer simply.
no. you can want different things today and still be friends.
picoboi, make it open.
what would you like to open? are we talking about a book, a door, or something else?
i wanted you to change a story sentence from the door was closed to the door was open.
the door was open.
say my last request simply.
change the story sentence the door was closed to the door was open.
did my first message give that context?
no. make it open did not say which object or whether you wanted a writing change. asking helped me find out what you wanted.
say it simply.
asking helped me find out that you wanted to change a sentence, rather than open a real door.
now put the open door into a story without saying someone broke it.
the door was open when the child came home. she called to her father, who answered from the kitchen. he had left it open while carrying a container inside.
does open tell you broken?
no. open and broken are different details. the story says why the door was open and does not say it was broken.
